titleStmt.title: Schedulability and Optimal Checkpoint Placement for Real-Time Multi-Tasks

analytic.title: Schedulability and Optimal Checkpoint Placement for Real-Time Multi-Tasks

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: An optimal checkpoint strategy for fault-tolerance in real-time systems is addressed in this paper. We consider multiple real-time tasks with arbitrary periods that are scheduled by Rate Monotonic (RM) algorithm. Equidistant checkpointing is maintained for each kind of task, while the width of checkpoint intervals is different with respect to the task. We propose a method to determine the optimal checkpoint interval for each task so that the probability of completing all the tasks is maximized. Whenever a fault occurs to a checkpoint interval of a task, the execution time of the task would be prolonged by rollback and re-execution of checkpoints. Our scheme includes the schedulability test to examine whether a task can be completed with an extended execution time. A numerical experiment demonstrates the applicability of the proposed scheme.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In this study, we focus on determining checkpoint intervals for real-time multi-tasks. As a technique for improving the reliability and availability of fault-tolerant computing systems, checkpoint and rollback recovery has been an active area of research in real-time systems [1], [2]. The key problem of checkpointing is how to determine strategies for checkpoint placement to meet optimally a prescribed objective of the system performance. Various mathematical models of checkpoint scheduling, with different objectives, have been formulated to address the problem. Among notable previous criteria are time loss for a computation restart after system failures [1], system availability [3], the total expected cost [4], [5], and the task response time [6].

The objective of this paper is to present an off-line algorithm for checkpoint placement based on the probability of task completion. We assume that the considered realtime system executes multiple independent tasks that are scheduled by the Rate Monotonic (RM) algorithm. The system is subject to transient faults with Poisson distribution. Checkpoints are inserted at a constant interval in the execution of a task; the width of the interval is different for each task in general. Every fault is supposed to be detected at the checkpoint that comes first after the fault occurrence.

Under the checkpoint scheme, the execution time of a task job is prolonged by re-executing the checkpoint intervals that are attacked by transient faults. Each job of the same task may have a different execution time with respect to its period. This implies that conventional schedulability tests in the literature [7] are hardly applicable to validate that the real-time system can meet all its hard deadlines with a given set of re-executed checkpoint intervals. Therefore, it is very difficult, if not impossible, to derive the probability of task completion for any possible combination of re-execution numbers of checkpoint intervals. Owing to this inherent complexity, few researches [8] have tackled the checkpoint placement problem within the framework of probabilistic optimization.

The significance of our work lies in that we succeed in deriving an explicit formula of the probability that all the tasks are successfully completed with a given set of checkpoint intervals. The probability computation presented in this paper also includes the schedulability analysis with respect to the numbers of re-executed checkpoint intervals. By removing from the probability computation any combination of checkpoint intervals that violates schedulability condition, we develop a complete form of probability of task completion, which serves as the objective function for the optimization problem solving the checkpoint interval for each task.

div.head: II. MODELING
div.p: As mentioned, we assume that the task set is scheduled by the RM algorithm, which assigns higher priorities to tasks with shorter periods.
We consider a uniprocessor system with a set of m real-time periodic tasks T ØT 1 , T 2 , . . . , T m Ù with hard deadlines. For further usage, let
div.formula: T i ØT 1 , T 2 , . . . , T i Ù (1 i m). Each task is described by T i Ôp i , e i Õ,
div.p: where p i is the period and e i is the execution time T i has with no checkpoint placed. The relative deadline of a task is assumed to be equal to the period. Without no loss of generality, the tasks are enumerated in decreasing order of priority, i.e., p 1 p 2 ¤ ¤ ¤ . Note that, unlike the previous studies [8], we do not premise any algebraic condition on the periods of the tasks, that is, a period is not necessarily an integer multiple of another period.

Let the least common multiple of p 1 , p 2 , . . . , p m be H and call it the hyperperiod of T. Since the RM algorithm is a static periodic scheduling, the same scheduling result will repeat in every interval of H. Hence, considering only the time range Ö0, H× serves as solving the problem in the entire time domain. In this paper we thus focus on the range Ö0, H×.

Each task T i is a sequence of jobs J i, j , j 1, . . . , v i , where v i Hßp i is the number of p i 's in the hyperperiod H. Each job is released in-phased with its period, i.e, J i, j is released at the instant Ô j ¡ 1Õp i . d i, j , the absolute deadline of J i, j , is thus

div.p: Let e i, j denote the execution time of J i, j . As mentioned, the value of e i, j changes depending on the number of re-executed checkpoint intervals, which is in turn determined by transient faults occurring in the period of the job. We employ equidistant checkpointing, so the checkpoints are equally distributed throughout the execution time of the process. Note, however, that the equidistant strategy is engaged only in the process of each task, that is, the width of the checkpoint interval is different with respect to the kind of tasks.

Let Δ i and n i be the checkpoint interval and the number of checkpoints inserted in a period of task T i , respectively. Also, denote by t cp the checkpoint overhead that is the time to store the processor's states and to conduct fault detection procedures. A checkpoint interval consists of the execution time divided by n i plus the overhead of the checkpoint placed at the end of the interval:
div.formula: Δ i e i n i t cp .(2)
div.p: Recall that the execution time of each job is different according to the number of re-executed checkpoint intervals by transient faults. To express the number of re-execution for each task in the entire range Ö0, H×, let us define the 1 ¢ v i re-execution vector L i such that

div.p: where l i, j denotes the number of re-executed checkpoint intervals in the jth period of T i , i.e., when executing job J i, j . l i, j is not necessarily equal to the number of transient faults occurring in the corresponding checkpoint interval. Even if more than one fault may occur to a checkpoint interval, the system will take a single rollback to the previous checkpoint, so the number of re-executed checkpoint intervals rises only by one. e i, j is the actual execution time of J i, j that includes both the checkpoint overhead and re-executed intervals. Since n i checkpoints are placed in a period of T i , the total amount of time required by the checkpoints is n i t cp . Further, considering the re-execution vector L i defined in (3), l i, j intervals are reexecuted in the period of J i, j . Hence, e i, j is given by e i, j e i n i t cp l i, j Δ i .

div.head: III. DETERMINING SCHEDULABILITY
div.p: The more checkpoint intervals are rolled back and reexecuted in a period of a job, the less slack time of the period will be available to the job in the period. As rollback and re-execution continues, there comes a moment that the RM algorithm is not validated any longer, i.e., the slack time becomes negative. Hence it is a prerequisite for deriving the probability of task completion to develop a schedulability test that determines whether all the tasks T meet their deadlines with a given set of re-execution vectors.

A direct scheme of the schedulability test is to check whether the slack times of all the task jobs are nonnegative. The characteristic of the RM algorithm makes the schedulability test simpler. To obtain the slack time of a task in a period, we have to consider only the time slot in the period occupied by the tasks with higher priority.

Before deriving the slack time, we introduce some parameters used in the scheduling theory relevant to this study. More detailed explanation can be found in [7] and [9] (some terminologies are modified for our convenience).

Effective deadline d e i, j : The effective deadline of a job is equal to the minimum value among its given absolute deadline and the effective deadline of all of its successors. Without a successor, the effective deadline is equal to its given absolute deadline. This definition is necessary to characterize a situation that a job should be completed earlier than its original deadline whenever a job with higher priority occupies a time range including the absolute deadline. Cumulative slack time σ i, j Ô0Õ: σ i, j Ô0Õ denotes the slack time of task T i computed from the initial time 0 until the jth period. σ i, j Ô0Õ is equal to the difference between the total available time in Ô0, d i, j × and the total amount of time required to complete J i,1 , . . . , J i, j and all the jobs of T i that are ready in this interval and have the same or earlier deadlines than the jobs of T i . Level-i busy interval Ôt s , t e ×: Ôt s , t e × begins at an instant t s when (i) all jobs in T i released before the instant have been completed and (ii) a job in T i is released. The interval ends at the first instant t e after t s when all the jobs in T i released since t s are completed. In other words, Ôt s , t e × is an interval where the processor is "busy" all the time executing jobs with priority i or higher. div.head: IV. CHECKPOINT PLACEMENT
div.p: We assume that all the transient faults are detectable and occur according to a Poisson process with rate λ. We also assume that no fault occurs during rollback and state retrieving processes. Let p i be the probability that no fault occurs in a checkpoint interval Δ i of task T i , and let q i be the probability that at least one fault occurs in the range. p i and q i are given by p i e ¡λΔ i , q i 1 ¡ e ¡λΔ i .

Then the processor will pass through n i l i, j checkpoints in total until accomplishing job J i, j , among which no fault is detected in n i checkpoints. In particular, in any case of completing J i, j , the last checkpoint, i.e., the (n i l i, j )th visited one, will end with no fault. Otherwise, the processor should be rolled back and re-execute the last checkpoint interval, which implies that the total number of checkpoints the processor passes through would be more than n i l i, j .
